title: Wall Drawing Series: Jitish Kallat
summary: Jitish Kallat at the Menil Drawing Institute, Houston. Photo: Sarah Hobson The Menil Collection has commissioned artist Jitish Kallat to create a site-specific wall drawing for the entry space of the Menil Drawing Institute. Born in Mumbai, where he continues to live and work, Kallat is a leading figure in contemporary Indian art. His work often probes the intersections of the intimate and the immense, weaving together references to history, science, philosophy, and the cosmic scale of time. Wall Drawing Series: Jitish Kallat is curated by Edouard Kopp, John R. Eckel, Jr. Foundation Chief Curator, Menil Drawing Institute. The series began in 2018 as part of the Institute’s commitment to seeking new approaches to the form and language of drawing. Past participants include Marc Bauer, Mel Bochner, Roni Horn, Marcia Kure, Gladys Nilsson, Ronny Quevedo, and Jorinde Voigt. Over the past three decades, Jitish Kallat has developed a multifaceted practice spanning drawing, painting, sculpture, photography, and time-based media. A recurring approach in his work involves shifting focal lengths across space and time, from the intimate to the cosmic and the present to the historic. Kallat has presented solo exhibitions at the Art Institute of Chicago, the Art Gallery of New South Wales (Sydney), the Frist Art Museum (Nashville), the Philadelphia Museum of Art, and the National Gallery of Modern Art (New Delhi). His work has also been presented at Tate Modern (London), Martin-Gropius-Bau (Berlin), and Mori Art Museum (Tokyo) and at the biennales of Venice, Gwangju, Havana, Bangkok, Curitiba, and Kyiv. Having served as curator and artistic director of the 2014 edition, Kallat is currently president of the Kochi-Muziris Biennale.

title: Fragility
summary: Ann Hamilton, in collaboration with Dieu Donné, poche, 2014. Paper, sheep wool, and thread, 24 × 18 in. (61 × 45.7 cm). The Menil Collection, Houston, Gift of Dieu Donné. © Ann Hamilton. Photo: Caroline Philippone This display highlights paper itself—and its incongruous and variable characteristics—as an artistic material. Included are works that present a range of processes, as well as paper sculptures and found papers that imbue a finished work with an additional sense of history and place. Among the artists featured in the exhibition, Lee Krasner relentlessly critiqued her own art, often destroying drawings only to reconstitute them as abstract collages. Ann Hamilton also brought papers together in surprising ways. In her collaborative work poche, 2014, she stitched soft wool between sheets of handmade paper to reflect on the pocket as both storage and protection for the body. Zarina grieved the loss of her husband and her native India by painstakingly puncturing paper with a needle to form intricate compositions. Fragility is curated by Kelly Montana, Associate Curator, Menil Drawing Institute.

title: Modern and Contemporary
summary: The Menil Collection’s modern and contemporary holdings encompass a vast array of movements, materials, and styles, spanning the late 19th century to the present. Currently on display are more than forty paintings, sculptures, drawings, and photographs from the collection, alongside important loans. Recent acquisitions on view include works by Sam Gilliam, Alice Neel, and Lynda Benglis. Included in the presentation is John Chamberlain’s monumental American Tableau, 1984. First installed outdoors at Seagram Plaza in New York City, the structure is comprised of fourteen components, made from the sculptor’s signature material of scrap metal auto parts. When the Menil opened its doors in 1987, American Tableau was among the twenty-three sculptures by Chamberlain on display in an inaugural exhibition. In their lifetimes, the de Menils were avid collectors of modern and contemporary artists. Many of the works in the collection reflect the couple’s dedication to cultivating close relationships with those artists, including Andy Warhol, Niki de Saint Phalle, Robert Rauschenberg, and Yves Klein. The museum continues to actively expand its holdings in this area, and the current display includes noteworthy new acquisitions. Installation view at the Menil Collection, Houston. Photo: Caroline Philippone

title: Surrealism
summary: The Menil Collection is home to one of the largest and most significant collections of Surrealism in the United States. A suite of permanent collection galleries is dedicated to this artistic movement, which began in France in the mid-1920s. The installation includes thematic rooms that highlight the Surrealists’ interest in bodily fragmentation and the double. Others explore Surrealism’s influence on postwar art movements, including Art Informel and Pop assemblage. Single-artist galleries dedicated to Max Ernst, René Magritte, and Joan Miró complete the display. John and Dominique de Menil’s involvement with Surrealism began in the early 1930s when, shortly after their marriage, they commissioned Ernst to paint a portrait of Dominique. While charmed by the artist, they were taken aback by his strange creation—a radically spare composition of a face painted in three-quarter profile, situated against a navy-blue background and surrounded by floating shells—and relegated it to a back closet for many years. In 1946, they considered it again. In the intervening time, they had purchased their first modest works by major modernists, including Paul Cézanne and Pablo Picasso, and their tastes had evolved. It was as if we were seeing the painting for the first time, our eyes open at last. The couple eventually became the most important United States-based champions of three artists closely associated with Surrealist movement: Victor Brauner, Max Ernst, and René Magritte. In a mark of their dedication, they initiated and funded the catalogues raisonnés of Ernst and Magritte and sponsored numerous exhibitions of their work. Today, Surrealism remains a core part of the Menil's holdings.

title: Africa
summary: The Menil Collection’s African galleries feature examples of masks, figural statues, musical instruments, textiles, architectural elements, and other forms of visual culture primarily from West and Central Africa. An introductory gallery explores the shared visual histories between Africa and Europe after the 15th century. European imagery of the continent and its people, and representations of Europeans by African artists, point to a long, uneven history of encounters. The paintings, sculptures, and works on paper in this section provoke conversations about the corrosive histories of slavery, colonialism, and racism and foster a deeper appreciation for artworks from different African peoples seen in adjoining galleries. The museum’s holdings from Africa include more than 900 works dating from the 3rd millennium BCE to the 20th century that represent cultural histories and visual traditions of roughly half of the continent’s 54 countries. John and Dominique de Menil acquired some their first examples of African art in the early 1930s while living in Paris, the cosmopolitan center of France’s vast colonial empire. The monumental exhibition Exposition Coloniale Internationale (Paris Colonial Exposition) in the Bois de Vincennes, probably prompted the young couple’s purchase in 1932 of a mask (mukudj or mukuyi) from the Punu-Shira or Lumbu peoples of Gabon (then Afrique équatoriale française). Following their early exposure, the de Menils acquired most of the African collection between the 1950s and 1970s while living in Houston and New York. This period corresponded with African-led intellectual and political movements that culminated in the downfall of colonial governments. The same period saw the dramatic increase in the popularity and circulation of African art among collectors in the United States. title: 4th–18th Century Europe
summary: Reflecting the varied and eclectic intellectual inclinations of John and Dominique de Menil is a wide-ranging collection of art from the 4th to 18th centuries, originating in Europe and the parts of North Africa and Western Asia controlled by the Roman and later Byzantine Empires. These holdings include 1,375 works from the Medieval and Byzantine era (4th–mid 15th century) and more than 7,000 objects from the Early Modern era (late 15th–late 18th century), during which many of the characteristics of the modern world emerged, among them scientific inquiry, global exploration and colonization, humanism, and nation-states. The Menil’s collection of Byzantine, Post-Byzantine, and Russian icons is widely regarded by scholars as one of the most important in the United States. These holdings are displayed in a darkened, intimate space designed to evoke a chapel. The icon collection embodies the aesthetic and spiritual values that guided the de Menils throughout their lives as collectors. Rooms dedicated to the broader Medieval and Early Modern eras are presented adjacent to the icon gallery. On display are objects that illustrate the daily life of medieval Byzantium, featuring Byzantine church furnishings and a smaller collection of Western European works like reliquaries, architectural fragments, and religious statuary. Medieval art and artifacts are situated alongside noteworthy paintings, prints, sculpture, and decorative arts from the 15th to 18th century. Selections include significant paintings by or attributed to Christopher Amberger, François Clouet, Jean-Baptiste Greuze, Christian Luycks, François de Nomé, and Anthony van Dyck.

title: Pacific Islands
summary: The Menil Collection stewards a significant collection of more than 300 works from the Pacific Islands. Masks, figural sculptures, architectural elements, and musical instruments, primarily from the regions of Melanesia and Polynesia, are regularly on view in a dedicated gallery and in A Surrealist Wunderkammer. In this gallery, a monumental slit gong (atingting kon) and tree fern grade figures (mage or bwerang) from Vanuatu are an imposing presence. The composition emulates the ceremonial space or clearing (nasara) in which name- or title-taking rituals take place on the islands of Ambrym and Malakula. Conspicuously occupying the center of the gallery, the group denotes a separation between the display objects from Polynesia and Melanesia on opposite sides of the gallery. One section highlights the sophisticated wood carving of Polynesia with a “treasure box” (papahou) from the Māori and an incredibly rare drum (pahu ra) from the Austral Islands. Commemorative arts from Papua New Guinea and the neighboring island of New Ireland represent the visual culture of Melanesia. The memorial figure (uli) and vertical ceremonial pole (valik ekuar) on view are examples associated with the central New Ireland funerary traditions of malagan, which includes multiple weeks of communal exchanges of carvings, masks, and pigs. The Pacific Islands objects held by the museum are among the earliest collected by John and Dominique de Menil. In 1924, John de Menil was one of seven students selected by the French government and the Parisian Le Journal for a sponsored tour around the world. During his six-month long voyage, which included brief stays in Vanuatu, Tahiti, and Fiji, he collected examples of local textiles. In 1932, the de Menils purchased two painted bark textiles (maro) from French Surrealist Jacques Viot, who had recently returned from a collecting expedition in the Humboldt Bay and Lake Sentani regions of Papua, Indonesia. title: A Surrealist Wunderkammer
summary: A Surrealist Wunderkammer is an ongoing single-gallery exhibition devoted to the observations of human nature from the perspectives of Surrealism, an international art and literary movement started by André Breton, Paul Éluard, and others in France in the 1920s. Featuring more than 200 works, the installation draws from the museum’s collection as well as long-term loans from the de Menil family and the Rock Foundation. The exhibition includes masks, sculptures, musical instruments, photographic and moving-image technologies, paintings, prints, tourist curios, and other objects that informed the imagination, political aesthetic, and varied artistic practices of Surrealism. Originally opening in 1999 with the title Witnesses–A Surrealist Wunderkammer, the exhibition developed out of conversations between anthropologist Edmund S. Carpenter (1922–2011) and his mother-in-law, Dominique de Menil (1908–1997). The first title was a direct reference to wunderkammern (“wonder rooms”) or curiosity cabinets. Popularized in Europe by the 16th century, wunderkammern were storehouses and royal treasuries for displaying collections of art, natural marvels, and other strange or magical items, such as petrified wood or the long tooth of a narwhale. Alluding to these historical displays, circular brass tags engraved with numbers identify the works on view in the gallery. Carpenter’s motivation for the initial exhibition was to “reveal a common intelligence” that connected the collections of Indigenous arts and Surrealism assembled by the de Menil family during the 20th century. “The point—the intelligence—behind this,” he wrote, “is simply that what first appears as disorder, becomes order once the Surrealist vision is grasped.”

title: Outdoor Sculpture
summary: Throughout the Menil Collection’s campus, visitors can discover works by artists Michael Heizer, Ellsworth Kelly, Jim Love, Max Neuhaus, and Mark di Suvero. Michael Heizer (b. 1944) began creating immense earthworks in the 1960s. In 1968, for Nine Nevada Depressions, the artist dug nine large-scale trenches into a dry Nevada lakebed, which were then left to erode. Several of these forms were later recreated in weathering steel: Dissipate, Isolated Mass/Circumflex (#2), and Rift are three of the resulting works. Isolated Mass/Circumflex (#2) was sited and installed by the artist on the Menil’s front lawn in 1987. Heizer interrupted one of its sections with the central walkway in order to reinforce its identity as sculpture rather than a linear design element framed by the surrounding sidewalks. Dissipate is based on a chance composition of dropped matches, and Rift consists of a line that sharply turns along its course. The latter two works are sited in a gravel field designed by the artist east of the Menil Drawing Institute. Another work by the artist, Charmstone, hangs adjacent to the main building's front entrance. Ellsworth Kelly’s (1923–2015) Menil Curve is located at the Menil Drawing Institute entrance. The sculpture was commissioned specifically for the building and is one of the last public sculptures the artist created. The juxtaposition of the glossy white sculpture and the building’s exterior courtyard wall behind it creates the effect of a white-on-white relief. The subtle interplay between the two shades of white resonates with a long-standing line of inquiry in Kelly’s practice. Over several decades, the artist explored the varied effects of folded white paper and white-on-white collages. Houston artist Jim Love (1927–2005) made a series of sculptures in varying sizes in the shape of a toy jack. title: D’MBA: Beauty, Desire, and Collecting an African Mask
summary: Detail of Shoulder Mask (d’mba or nimba), late 19th-mid 20th century. Baga peoples, Guinea. Wood, 50 × 15 1/2 × 24 1/8 in. (127 × 39.4 × 61.3 cm). The Menil Collection, Houston. Photo: Paul Hester D’MBA: Beauty, Desire, and Collecting an African Mask is a focused research and exhibition project examining the large wood headdresses commonly referred to as d’mba, nimba, or yamban among the Baga, Nalu, and neighboring peoples living in Guinea, West Africa. Worn and performed by men for ceremonies and public celebrations that mark significant moments in the cycle of life, the d’mba headdress is the sculptural embodiment of female personhood, sustenance (agricultural and maternal), physical beauty, and generational continuity. Shoulder Mask (d’mba or nimba), late 19th-mid 20th century. Baga peoples, Guinea. Wood, 50 × 15 1/2 × 24 1/8 in. (127 × 39.4 × 61.3 cm). The Menil Collection, Houston. Photo: Paul Hester During the mid-20th century, at the height of the international market for African art in the United States, the d’mba became one of the objects most coveted by collectors. D’MBA unites for the first time a significant group of headdresses on loan from several art museums in the United States, including Art Institute of Chicago, Baltimore Museum of Art, Davis Museum at Wellesley College, National Museum of African Art, and Yale University Art Gallery. The exhibition of these headdresses, which were acquired during the late 1950s by prominent collectors in the United States, occasions a rare opportunity to pursue a thorough study of these icons of African art at the intersections of mask-making, colonial art education, independence-era cultural politics and religious iconoclasm in Guinea, and the international art market.

title: Wall Drawing Series: Gladys Nilsson
summary: Gladys Nilsson’s site-specific work titled Drawing presented fantastical, hybrid beings all surrounding one monumental figure engaged in the act of drawing. A complex, garland-like arrangement of black-and-white characters soared overhead, entangled with one another, while the bystanders below, set apart by gentle color-toning, observed the scene. The bustling composition was marked by deft and fluid lines using a candy-colored palette of crayon, graphite, and acrylic paint and marker pens. Nilsson’s whimsical creation embodied her distinctive sense of humor and levity while taking viewers on a journey through the peculiar beauty of the human experience. title: Robert Rauschenberg: Fabric Works of the 1970s
summary: On the occasion of the one hundredth birthday of American artist Robert Rauschenberg (1925–2008), the Menil Collection presented an exhibition that looked at the artist’s expressive and conceptual use of fabric as a sculptural medium. title: Lines of Resolution: Drawing at the Advent of Television and Video
summary: Lines of Resolution: Drawing at the Advent of Television and Video explored the relationship between drawing, television, and video from the late 1950s into the 1980s. Personal electronics became widely available during this era and soon made their way into artists’ studios. These electric screens became a source of artistic imagery, a surface for inscription, and a device that could be manipulated to generate entirely new kinds of drawing. title: The Space Between Looking and Loving: Francesca Fuchs and the de Menil House
summary: In 1970, John de Menil wrote to German classical archeologist Dr. Werner Fuchs (1927–2016) seeking to identify the subject of a Roman male torso in his collection. Forty-nine years later, Francesca Fuchs’s discovery of black-and-white photographs depicting the marble torso in her father’s personal effects in Oxford, England, led the Houston-based painter to find the original letter in the museum archives. This exhibition was the artist’s response to the unanswered letter and unexpected familial connection. Featuring new work by Fuchs and selections from the museum’s collection and archives, the exhibition explored the affective power and relational histories of objects in domestic settings, especially those of the de Menil house in Houston, Texas. The Space Between Looking and Loving: Francesca Fuchs and the de Menil House at the Menil Collection, Houston. Video: Jay Clark Films Born in London and raised in Münster, Germany, Francesca Fuchs moved to Houston in 1996 as a fellow for the Core Program at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston. During her thirty-year career in Houston and internationally, Fuchs’s work has been a process of honing extended reflections on the nature of everyday objects and illuminating their fundamental truths. Her portraits of objects are re-paintings of paintings, prints, photographs that resist and reconsider their accepted signals of cultural importance, particularly as they relate to the intimacies of life. Fuchs’s work has been included in exhibitions organized by the Institute of Contemporary Art, London; The Whitechapel Art Gallery, London; The Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth; Contemporary Arts Museum Houston; Art Museum of Southeast Texas, Beaumont; The Museum of Fine Arts, Houston; The Suburban, Oak Park, Illinois. In 2018, Art League Houston recognized Fuchs as Texas Artist of the Year.

title: Foyer Installation: René Magritte
summary: An installation in the main building foyer celebrates the Menil Collection’s extraordinary holdings of work by the Belgian Surrealist, René Magritte (1898–1967). It focuses on a core group of paintings from the 1950s and ’60s, in which the artist rendered impossible situations with virtuosic precision and uncanny clarity. Now regarded as icons of the Surrealist movement, these paintings were purchased within a couple years of their making by the museum’s founders, John and Dominique de Menil. The de Menils were Magritte’s most important champions in the United States. Beginning in the late 1940s, they bought dozens of his artworks, lent to and organized major exhibitions of his work, and led the publication of a significant, six-volume catalogue raisonné. Through these and other activities, the de Menils fundamentally shaped the artist’s reception and reputation in the postwar American art world. In 2024, the Menil Collection continued this legacy by being a major lender to the first-ever retrospective of Magritte’s work in Australia, including the loan of the paintings in this display.

title: Animals, Monsters, and Creatures from the Collection
summary: This display in the west hallway takes its inspiration from Constant Companions, an exhibition curated by Dominique de Menil and Jermayne MacAgy for the University of St. Thomas in 1964. The show explored monsters in art— “ambivalent, protective, or threatening,” as Dominique wrote in her introduction to the catalogue. She brought a particular interest to animal-human hybrids, their iconography and “complex and ambivalent” meaning. Crossing time periods and geographies, Constant Companions encompassed 300 objects, from paintings, bronze sculptures, and carvings to book illustrations, icons, and vases. The exhibition was met with wide acclaim, covered by NBC News, The New York Times, Vogue, Art in America, and Newsweek, which deemed it “one of the year’s best off-beat shows.” Several outlets noted that it opened to the public one day before Halloween—mounting, in the words of a Houston Chronicle reviewer, “an artistic contribution to these days of black cats and cauldron bubbles.” For the dramatic installation, the gallery space was painted black and partitioned like a maze, with artworks brightly spot lit in cave-like vestibules. Writing to a friend in advance of the opening, John de Menil described it as “an exhibition of monsters, evil or endearing, from 1,000 B.C. to yesterday morning, from Egypt to Peru, from Italy to Siberia.” According to the Houston Post, it became known among locals as simply “The Monster Show.” Paying homage to the 1960s show, this display brings together a selection of paintings and objects that highlight artists’ perennial fascination with fantastic and monstrous creatures.

title: What drawing can be: four responses
summary: Four artists stretch the boundaries of drawing and offer new characterizations of what drawing can be. This exhibition featured site-specific installations by Jillian Conrad, Teresita Fernández, Tony Lewis, and Constantin Luser. Each artist had an individual gallery space to explore the experimental potential of the medium, its boundaries, and its connections with other arts, such as sculpture and architecture. Drawings that expand beyond a sheet of paper have a rich history within the 20th century. Examples include Alexander Calder and his wire sculptures from the 1930s and artists of the 1960s, like Dorothea Rockburne and Sol LeWitt, who pushed the parameters of the medium to include text, folded papers, and wall drawings. Eluding labels and limitations, whether they be in terms of material, scale, or ephemerality, the artists in this exhibition will reveal the continuing relevance, agility, and vitality of drawing and how it remains a rich and generative area of investigation. Jillian Conrad (b. 1970) explores questions of materiality and intangibility. Her sculptures and works on paper often engage aspects of the landscape and everyday materials with the goal of locating thresholds between the visible and invisible. Conrad lives and works in Houston. Jillian Conrad in What drawing can be: four responses at the Menil Drawing Institute, Houston. Video: Jay Clark Films
